strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: revisits actor parameterization/architecture as an underexplored lever in on-policy RL, connecting classification-style objectives (used successfully for value learning) to policy learning.

Rigorous theoretical contribution: Proposition 4.1 provides a clean, fully proven comparison of REINFORCE gradient variance between Gaussian and categorical policies, giving a principled (if stylized) explanation for why categorical actors may exhibit lower gradient variance, especially as Gaussian std shrinks during training.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 5 Gym locomotion tasks, 10 ManiSkill state-based tasks, and 5 ManiSkill RGB tasks, with consistent 2x2 factorial ablation (discrete vs continuous x regularized vs MLP network) isolating the individual and combined effects of policy parameterization and architecture.

The loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) is a well-designed control experiment that convincingly disentangles the benefit of the discretized action representation from the cross-entropy-style optimization objective, showing the latter is the dominant factor.

Additional scaling studies (actor width, number of bins) and comparisons against strong off-policy/model-based baselines (TD3, TD-MPC2) add useful practical insight and situate the method relative to the broader continuous-control literature.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, environment descriptions, and normalization procedures are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: the categorical actor idea builds directly on Tang & Agrawal (2020)/Zhu et al. (2024), and the regularized residual+LayerNorm architecture is explicitly adapted from SimBa/BroNet-style designs (the paper itself states the contribution is not a new network module). The paper is primarily a careful empirical combination/ablation study rather than a fundamentally new method.

No empirical comparison against the more sophisticated ordinal or unimodal (Poisson-based) discretized actor parameterizations from the closely related prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024), despite these being the most directly comparable baselines for the discretization component; the paper only compares to a 'simplest baseline' softmax discretization, leaving open whether RN-D's advantage would persist against stronger discretization schemes.

Performance is shown to be quite sensitive to the number of bins K (Appendix C.4), yet no principled method for choosing K is proposed; this introduces an additional hyperparameter whose optimal value seems task/architecture dependent, undermining the 'simple drop-in change' framing.

The SOTA/wall-clock comparisons against TD3 and TD-MPC2 (Appendix C.1) are conducted only on 2 of the 20 evaluated tasks and across non-identical hardware (H800/RTX5090 vs A200), and TD-MPC2 is evaluated with only 3 seeds versus 5 for the proposed method, weakening the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract.

Proposition 4.1 relies on a simplified one-step REINFORCE toy setting with constant returns and a fixed covariance; the extrapolation of this insight to the full PPO clipped-surrogate setting with learned, state-dependent variance is asserted qualitatively but not formally justified or empirically verified beyond a single aggregate variance plot (Fig. 4).

The paper lacks an explicit Limitations section; issues surfaced in the paper's own ablations (bin-count sensitivity, non-monotonic returns with actor width, entropy coefficient fixed to 0) are not synthesized into a discussion of when the method might fail or require tuning.
The Impact Statement is boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any ethical or societal considerations specific to the work.

strengths: The paper provides a clean, well-motivated analysis connecting categorical actor updates to a cross-entropy-like objective, paralleling recent findings on classification-based value learning, which is a reasonable conceptual framing.
A gradient-variance analysis (Proposition 4.1) is provided with a full proof, offering some theoretical grounding, even if in a simplified toy setting.
The empirical evaluation spans a reasonably broad set of benchmarks (MuJoCo locomotion, ManiSkill state-based, ManiSkill RGB-based), with multiple seeds and bootstrap confidence intervals.
The loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2), which disentangles the effect of discretization from the effect of the cross-entropy-like objective, is a thoughtful and informative control experiment.
Additional ablations on actor width and number of discretization bins provide some useful practical guidance on hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: both ingredients of the proposed method (discretized categorical actors and residual/LayerNorm MLP architectures) are directly taken from prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024; Lee et al. 2024 SimBa; Nauman et al. 2025 BroNet). The paper explicitly states the architecture itself is not novel, leaving the core contribution as a fairly straightforward combination of two existing ideas, which is a modest contribution for a main-track submission.

The paper claims 'state-of-the-art performance' but never empirically compares against the actual closest related discretized-actor baselines it cites as most relevant (ordinal/Poisson-based unimodal discretized policies from Tang & Agrawal 2020 and Zhu et al. 2024). Only a plain softmax categorical baseline (MLP-D) is used, so the SOTA claim is unsubstantiated relative to the true state of the art in discretized actors.

The comparison to TD3/TD-MPC2 (Appendix C.1) is weak: only 2 tasks, TD-MPC2 uses only 3 seeds versus 5 for the main method, and the hardware setup differs across methods (different GPU generations), undermining the reliability of the wall-clock claims.

The theoretical result (Prop 4.1) analyzes a simplified one-step REINFORCE setting with a constant, action-independent return and no advantage normalization/baseline subtraction, which is not representative of practical PPO training (with GAE, clipping, and advantage normalization already explicitly used in the actual experiments). The qualitative insight (Gaussian gradient variance blows up as σ→0) is also a well-known phenomenon, limiting the novelty of this analysis.

Inspection of the full per-task results (Fig. 8) shows several tasks (e.g., PickCubeSO100-v1, LiftPegUpright-v1, RollBall-v1, PushCube-v1) where RN-D does not clearly outperform or is comparable to/worse than baselines, which is in tension with the paper's framing of 'consistent gains' in the main text and abstract.

No analysis of computational overhead (extra parameters/FLOPs/wall-clock per step) introduced by the deeper regularized residual actor and the K=41-way categorical output heads relative to the shallow MLP baselines, making it hard to assess whether gains are compute-matched.

The limitations discussion is minimal, essentially folded into generic 'future work' bullet points in the conclusion, and the Impact Statement is boilerplate without any substantive engagement with potential downsides (e.g., increased compute cost, discretization-induced control granularity issues in safety-critical settings).

Entropy coefficient is fixed to 0 across all experiments; given that categorical and Gaussian policies have very different intrinsic exploration/entropy behavior, this choice could bias comparisons and is not justified or ablated.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated framing that connects the success of classification-style objectives in critic/value learning (distributional RL, cross-entropy value losses) to the actor side of on-policy RL, offering a coherent conceptual lens for revisiting policy parameterization.

Includes a theoretical contribution (Proposition 4.1) with a full proof comparing per-dimension REINFORCE gradient variance between Gaussian and categorical policies, giving some principled grounding for the empirical gains.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 20 tasks across three benchmark families (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state-based, ManiSkill RGB-based), with results averaged over 5 seeds and bootstrap confidence intervals reported.

Well-designed ablations that help disentangle the sources of improvement: the loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) convincingly shows that the categorical likelihood/cross-entropy objective—not discretization alone—drives most of the gains; additional studies on network width scaling and bin-count sensitivity add useful nuance.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, environment descriptions, and architecture specifications in the appendix.
Complementary diagnostic analyses (policy-gradient variance curves, SNR vs. performance correlation) strengthen the narrative link between the proposed design choices and optimization stability.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the two core ingredients (factorized categorical/discretized actors, and residual+LayerNorm MLP backbones with inverted bottlenecks) are both drawn directly from prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024; SimBa; BroNet); the contribution is primarily an empirical combination and a 'rediscovery' of classification-style benefits for actors rather than a new method.

The main experiments deliberately use plain uniform-bin softmax discretization and omit comparison against the more sophisticated ordinal/unimodal discretized actors from the cited prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024) in the main results, so the claim of 'state-of-the-art performance' is not substantiated against the most relevant discretized-actor baselines.

Theoretical analysis in Proposition 4.1 relies on a strongly simplified one-step REINFORCE setting with a state-independent constant return and ignores PPO's clipping/importance-ratio mechanics in the actual variance derivation, limiting how directly it explains the observed empirical behavior under full PPO training.

Comparisons against strong continuous-control baselines (TD3, TD-MPC2) are restricted to only two tasks (Humanoid-v4, StackCube-v1) and differ in hardware/training paradigm (on-policy vs. off-policy/model-based), making the 'state-of-the-art' claims in the abstract only weakly supported.

The bin-count ablation (Appendix C.4) shows that performance is quite sensitive to the number of discretization bins and that the optimum is task-dependent, which undercuts the framing of the method as a straightforward 'drop-in' replacement and suggests additional tuning burden in practice.

No explicit, dedicated limitations section; the discussion of weaknesses is folded into the conclusion as 'future directions' rather than a critical assessment of when/why the method might fail (e.g., on much higher-dimensional action spaces, with correlated action dimensions, or in off-policy-friendly regimes).
Figures report bootstrap confidence intervals but no formal statistical significance testing is performed to support claims of consistent superiority across tasks/seeds.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly connects on-policy actor optimization to a classification-style (cross-entropy) view versus a regression-style (squared-error) view, providing a coherent conceptual framing for why discretized categorical actors combined with architectural improvements from supervised learning should help.

Proposition 4.1 gives a clean, interpretable theoretical result comparing REINFORCE gradient variance for Gaussian vs. categorical policies in a simplified one-step setting, with a proof in the appendix, offering some formal grounding for the empirical claims.

The empirical evaluation is broad: three on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), three benchmark families (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state-based, ManiSkill RGB-based), and multiple seeds with confidence intervals, showing consistent improvements of RN-D over Gaussian and standard-MLP baselines across most settings.

The loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) is a valuable design that disentangles the effect of discretized action representation from the effect of the cross-entropy-like objective, strengthening the causal claim that the classification-style loss (not just discretization) drives the improvement.

Additional ablations on actor-network scaling, bin-count sensitivity, gradient-variance/SNR analysis, and runtime overhead provide a reasonably thorough characterization of the method's behavior and practical cost.
Comparisons to representative off-policy baselines (TD3, TD-MPC2) and wall-clock analysis help contextualize the practical value of the approach beyond only on-policy competitors.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a combination of two largely known ingredients (categorical/discretized actors from Tang & Agrawal 2020 and Zhu et al. 2024; residual+LayerNorm MLP backbones from SimBa/BroNet), and the paper explicitly acknowledges it introduces no new architectural module, which limits originality.

The paper deliberately avoids comparison against the more sophisticated discretization schemes it cites as directly related work (ordinal parameterizations of Tang & Agrawal; unimodal/Poisson-based parameterizations of Zhu et al.), which could be stronger baselines/ablations than plain uniform softmax discretization; without these comparisons it is unclear whether RN-D's gains stem mainly from the regularized network or would be further amplified/diminished when combined with these more structured discretized actors.

Proposition 4.1 relies on a highly simplified one-step, constant-return REINFORCE setting that does not directly model the multi-epoch, clipped, advantage-weighted PPO updates used in the actual experiments, so its practical relevance to explaining the observed training dynamics is more suggestive than rigorously established.

Main results are reported primarily via aggregate learning-curve plots rather than numerical tables with exact final scores and confidence intervals, making precise quantitative comparison, effect-size assessment, and reproducibility checks harder for readers.

Hyperparameters (including entropy coefficient set to 0, and other defaults) are held fixed from existing codebases across all four actor variants without task-specific tuning; this raises the possibility that baselines (especially MLP-C, the dominant standard implementation) are undertuned relative to what practitioners typically use, potentially inflating the perceived gap.

The bin-count ablation shows that performance degrades noticeably as K grows large and the ideal range is fairly narrow and task-dependent, suggesting the method requires non-trivial tuning of discretization granularity, somewhat undercutting the “simple drop-in replacement” framing.

The actor-critic interaction is left unexplored (critic architecture is held fixed throughout), which is a reasonable scoping choice but limits the paper's ability to draw conclusions about jointly scaling networks in on-policy RL, an important aspect given the framing around network capacity and classification-style optimization.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three environment families (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state-based, ManiSkill RGB) and three on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), demonstrating that the proposed actor change is algorithm-agnostic.

The paper includes a reasonable set of ablations (loss-swap experiment isolating cross-entropy vs. squared-error objectives, bin-count sweep, actor-width scaling, gradient SNR/variance analysis) that attempt to disentangle which factors (discretization, architecture, objective) drive the gains.

A clean theoretical proposition formalizes the intuition that Gaussian policy gradients can have higher variance than categorical policy gradients as exploration (std) shrinks, providing some conceptual grounding for the empirical observations.
The writing is generally clear, the related work section is thorough, and the paper provides substantial implementation/hyperparameter details for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited originality: both ingredients of RN-D—discretized categorical actors (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024) and regularized residual/LayerNorm MLP backbones (SimBa, BroNet)—are directly imported from prior work. The paper explicitly declines to compare against the more sophisticated discretization schemes (ordinal, unimodal/Poisson) from the cited prior work, instead only benchmarking against a 'plain uniform discretization' baseline, which weakens the claim of achieving genuine state-of-the-art performance in this line of work.

The theoretical analysis (Proposition 4.1) is derived under a highly simplified, one-step REINFORCE toy setting with a constant, action-independent return and no PPO clipping/minibatching dynamics; it is unclear how much this result actually explains the observed training behavior in the full PPO/TRPO/SPO pipelines used in experiments.

The abstract's claim of 'achieving state-of-the-art results within on-policy RL' is not substantiated by comparison to actual published state-of-the-art on-policy baselines/numbers from the literature; comparisons are restricted to the authors' own re-implemented MLP-C/MLP-D/RN-C variants, which is a much narrower claim than what is advertised.

Statistical robustness is a concern: only 5 seeds are used, and several learning curves (e.g., StackCube, PushT, PickCubeSO100 in TRPO/SPO appendices) show very wide, overlapping confidence intervals, making some of the comparative claims (e.g., consistent superiority of RN-D) difficult to fully trust.

The bin-count ablation (Appendix C.4) shows that performance is quite sensitive to the choice of K, with optimal ranges varying by task; this undercuts the paper's framing of discretization as a simple, tuning-free 'drop-in replacement,' since practitioners would need to tune this additional hyperparameter per task.

Entropy coefficient is fixed at 0 across all experiments without justification or ablation, an unusual choice for PPO that could differentially affect exploration behavior between Gaussian and categorical actors and is not discussed as a potential confound.

The off-policy comparisons (TD3, TD-MPC2) in Appendix C.1 are limited to two tasks, run on different/unequal hardware (A200 vs RTX5090), and are only loosely contextualized rather than rigorously controlled, limiting the strength of any practical-efficiency claims drawn from them.

The critic architecture/capacity is held fixed across all actor variants, but no analysis is given of whether actor-critic capacity mismatch confounds comparisons, despite the paper itself noting actor-critic interaction as an open question for future work.

strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical evaluation across three on-policy algorithms (PPO, TRPO, SPO), three environment families (Gym locomotion, ManiSkill state, ManiSkill RGB), and multiple ablations (bin count, actor width, loss-swap, gradient variance/SNR), which is unusually thorough for an actor-design study in on-policy RL.

The loss-swap ablation (Appendix C.2) is a well-designed control that isolates the contribution of the cross-entropy-like objective from the mere effect of discretizing the action space, strengthening the causal story behind the proposed method.

The paper provides a theoretical proposition (4.1) bounding/relating gradient variance for Gaussian vs. categorical actors, giving some principled grounding to the empirical observation that discretized actors exhibit lower gradient variance, which is further supported empirically in Figure 5 and Figure 6.
Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: detailed hyperparameter tables, environment descriptions, and a described intent to release code.

The proposed method is simple, architecture-and-loss level (drop-in replacement for the actor), algorithm-agnostic, and shown to generalize across different on-policy surrogates (PPO/TRPO/SPO) and modalities (state/RGB), which increases its practical significance.
Runtime/throughput analysis (Tables 4-5) shows the method does not introduce meaningful computational overhead, addressing a natural practicality concern.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the discretized categorical actor idea is from prior work (Tang & Agrawal 2020; Zhu et al. 2024) and the regularized residual MLP architecture is borrowed essentially unchanged from SimBa/BroNet; the paper itself states its contribution is not a new network module. The main contribution is the combination and a systematic empirical/ablation study rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The paper does not compare against the more sophisticated discretized-actor baselines it cites as directly related (ordinal parameterization of Tang & Agrawal 2020, unimodal/Poisson parameterization of Zhu et al. 2024), despite explicitly acknowledging these as closely related alternatives; this omission makes it hard to assess whether the plain softmax discretization plus regularized network is actually better than prior discretization schemes, or just better than a vanilla MLP Gaussian baseline.

Proposition 4.1 compares gradient variance of a Gaussian policy w.r.t. its mean parameters against a categorical policy w.r.t. logits; these are different parameterizations with different dimensionalities (m vs mK) and the comparison depends on an arbitrarily chosen σ=1, which limits how much the bound actually explains the empirical results beyond a loose qualitative insight.

The bin-count ablation (Appendix C.4) shows that performance is quite sensitive to K and that the optimal value is task-dependent, which undercuts the 'simple drop-in replacement' narrative and introduces an additional hyperparameter that requires tuning per task.

The actor-scaling study (Appendix C.3) shows non-monotonic effects of increasing width (dh=512 sometimes performs worse than smaller widths), weakening the claim that the design is straightforwardly 'scalable.'

On vision-based ManiSkill tasks, the gap between RN-D and the MLP-C baseline is noticeably smaller, and the paper notes MLP-C is 'already competitive' in some cases, suggesting the benefits are strongest in low-dimensional state settings and may not transfer as strongly to richer perception-based settings.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art results within on-policy RL' is not substantiated by comparison to other published on-policy methods beyond the authors' own baselines (which share the same codebase/critic); all comparisons are essentially ablations of the authors' own pipeline rather than comparisons to competing published on-policy approaches.

Only 5 random seeds are used, and while bootstrap confidence intervals are reported, no formal significance testing is conducted, which is a modest statistical rigor concern given the relatively large number of task/ablation comparisons being drawn.
